finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, so any client can act as any user who holds a grant on a resource (authentication bypass for DELETE /files/<fid> and POST /files/<fid>/rename).
finding.source: request.headers.get("X-Session-User-Verified") in load_user (views.py:11), set on every request.
finding.sink: g.user used as the subject for ensure_allowed (views.py:17 -> acl.py:8-10) and is_allowed (views.py:25), gating del STORE[fid] (views.py:18) and f["name"] assignment (views.py:27).

trace.note: g.user set directly from raw request header, no signature, session, or trusted-proxy check
ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") called with attacker-chosen identity
is_allowed looks up grants[g.user] and tests action membership
abort(403) only when the spoofed identity has no grant
del STORE[fid] executes when the spoofed identity holds 'delete'
rename path: is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") with same spoofed identity

finding.guards_checked: No authentication in before_request; no session/cookie/HMAC on the header; per-resource ACL runs but trusts the identity it is given. Impact depends on deployment: safe only if an upstream gateway always overwrites or strips this header and the app is not directly reachable. Deployment config not present in the directory, so not confirmed. Runtime verification was attempted but blocked by a permission denial; this is static analysis only.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only control is ensure_allowed/is_allowed (acl.py:4-10), which does check and abort(403), but it authorizes whatever identity it is given. views.py:11 takes g.user from the raw X-Session-User-Verified header with no signature, session, or proxy check, and no authentication runs in before_request (views.py:9-11). The header is never set or stripped anywhere in the directory.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: views.py:11 sets g.user from a client-controlled header, and views.py:17-18 and views.py:25-27 use it as the ACL subject, so an anonymous client that sends the header as a user with a grant (acl.py:5) can delete or rename the file. The attacker is anonymous, and the only way this is blocked is if a deployment gateway always overwrites the header and the app is not directly reachable, which the directory does not show and so is unverified; the verdict rests on the code as given.

finding.claim: Existence oracle on file IDs: an unknown fid raises KeyError (HTTP 500) while an existing fid the caller cannot access returns 403, letting an unauthenticated caller enumerate valid file IDs.
finding.source: <fid> path parameter from any client (views.py:14-16, also views.py:22-24).
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup (views.py:16, views.py:24) distinguishing 500 from 403 responses.

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown fid, uncaught, yielding 500
abort(403) for known fid without grant

finding.guards_checked: ACL check runs before any mutation, so no unauthorised access; only existence is leaked. Impact depends on whether file IDs are guessable. Not runtime-verified.

verdict.guard_found: None blocks the oracle. views.py:16 and views.py:24 index STORE[fid] with no try/except or .get(), so an unknown fid raises an uncaught KeyError (Flask returns 500). For a known fid, views.py:17 calls ensure_allowed, which at acl.py:10 does abort(403) when is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is false; that check is effective, but it runs only after the lookup and only changes the response for known IDs. views.py:25-26 has the same 403 path for rename. The before_request hook (views.py:9-11) only sets g.user from a header and does not gate access. An anonymous caller gets g.user=None, which yields an empty grant list and therefore 403 on any existing file, so no login is needed.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: views.py:16 raises KeyError on an unknown fid (500), while views.py:17 with acl.py:10 abort(403) returns 403 for an existing fid the caller lacks grants for, and nothing between the request and these lines normalizes the two responses, so an anonymous caller can distinguish valid from invalid file IDs. Severity is low: it is an existence oracle only, and it depends on IDs being guessable.

finding.claim: Membership test on grants is a substring match when a user's grant value is a string, so a grant like 'undelete' or 'rewrite' satisfies action 'delete' or 'write'. Latent logic flaw; not reachable with current list-typed data.

trace.note: 'in' operator on str performs substring match; on list performs element match

finding.guards_checked: No type or normalisation check on grant values in this code. Requires grant data stored as strings, which this code does not produce. Not runtime-verified.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no type check or normalisation on grant values (acl.py:5, acl.py:9-10). The only reachability constraint is that grants are never written from request input: views.py:6 initialises STORE empty, and views.py:27 is the only write to a stored record and sets only f["name"] from request.json. Nothing in the provided code creates grants as strings.
verdict.reason: The trace at acl.py:5 is accurate (Python `in` on a str is a substring test), but the attacker cannot control grant values: views.py:27 writes only `name` from the request and no code path stores request-supplied grants, so the substring behaviour is an unreachable latent logic flaw, not an authorization vulnerability in this codebase.

finding.claim: rename handler does not validate request JSON or the name field: a missing 'name' key raises KeyError and returns 500; on pre-Flask-2.1 a non-JSON body yields None and a TypeError (500). Robustness issue, not an access bypass.
finding.sink: request.json["name"] subscript (views.py:27) and unvalidated write to f["name"].

trace.note: request.json["name"] raises when key missing or json is None
write ACL runs first, so only authorised callers reach this line

finding.guards_checked: Write ACL at views.py:25 precedes the parse, so unauthenticated callers cannot reach it. No type/length validation on name; no rendering sink in this code. Informational.

verdict.guard_found: views.py:25 `if not is_allowed(g.user, f, "write"): return ... 403` is a bool result that is tested and returns before the parse at views.py:27, so only callers with write permission reach line 27. No validation of the JSON body or the `name` value exists at views.py:27.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: views.py:25 is the write ACL check that returns 403 before views.py:27 runs `request.json["name"]`, so a missing key or null JSON body raises an unhandled exception (HTTP 500) for any authorized caller. The claimed effect is real, but it is a robustness defect reachable only by already-authorized writers, not a security vulnerability, so the finding's own "informational" framing holds.
